title: One-to-one counting
keyIdea: One-to-one correspondence means each object gets exactly one number name: touch or point once, say one word, then move on. Do not skip objects or say two numbers for the same object. The last number you say is how many there are.
familyTip: Line up five grapes. Ask: 'Touch each grape once and say one number.' Watch for a double-touch or a skip. Swap roles and let them catch your deliberate double-count.

visual.caption: Fair one-to-one count or not? Drag each clue, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: tap each object once while saying numbers, catch double-counts and skips, fix a messy count, and keep the last-number rule.

kid: When you count, give each thing exactly one number word.
Touch it once, say one number, then go to the next thing. Do not skip. Do not count the same thing twice.
If someone touches a grape twice and says two numbers, the count is too big.
The last number you say is how many things there are.
adult: EYFS / Year 1 number: one-to-one correspondence when counting a set. Stable order of number names plus one touch per object. Words: one-to-one, count, skip, double-count, last number, how many.
Common mistakes: double-counting the same object; skipping an object; counting spaces or gaps; treating the rhythm of saying numbers as enough without matching to objects.
In the lab your child taps each counter once, spots a double-count and a skip, rebuilds a fair count, links the last number to the total, then faces challenge traps for those slips.

practice.explain: One-to-one correspondence pairs each object with exactly one number name — no skips or doubles.

practice.prompt: If you touch the same grape twice…
choices: your count becomes too big
the count stays fair
you must skip the next grape
practice.hint: Two number words for one grape inflate the total.
practice.explain: Double-counting adds an extra number, so the total is larger than the set.

practice.prompt: There are {n} apples. You count fairly one-to-one. What is the last number you say?
practice.hint: In a fair count, the last number name equals how many objects there are.
practice.explain: With {n} apples counted one-to-one, the last number said is {n}.

practice.prompt: A tray has {n} grapes. Someone double-counts {k} of them (says two numbers for each of those). What total do they say?
practice.hint: Start from the true count, then add one extra number for each double-counted grape.
practice.explain: True count {n}, plus {k} extras from double-counts, makes {=n+k}.

practice.prompt: Skipping a grape in the middle…
choices: makes the said total too small
makes the said total too big
does not change anything
practice.hint: A missed object never gets a number name, so you stop too early.
practice.explain: A skip leaves an object without a number, so the last number is smaller than the set.

pool.prompt: Someone says 1, 2, 3, 4 for three toys by double-counting one. The true count is…
pool.hint: An inflated spoken total does not change how many toys sit there.
pool.explain: Three toys remain three even if a double-count made the spoken total 4.

pool.prompt: You count {n} beads one-to-one without skips. How many beads are there?
pool.hint: A fair count's last number equals the number of beads.
pool.explain: Fair one-to-one counting of {n} beads means there are {n}.

pool.prompt: A set has {n} counters. You skip {k}. What last number do you say?
pool.hint: Each skipped counter never gets a number, so subtract those from the true size.
pool.explain: {n} counters minus {k} skips leaves a spoken last number of {=n-k}.
